UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND FACULTY SENATE REPORT OF THE EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE September 2005 The Executive Committee met regularly during the summer 2005 and after consideration, the FSEC agreed to bring forward to the Faculty Senate recommendations for changes to the UNIVERSITY MANUAL regarding the establishment of a committee on the undergraduate initiative on the Providence Campus and the University.
Following are each of the recommendations with rationale.
I.PROVIDENCE CAMPUS UNDERGRADUATE INITIATIVE COMMITTEE.
Background The Faculty Senate approved the establishment of a committee to provide oversight for the new Providence Campus Undergraduate Initiative, which is scheduled to begin in Fall 2006. (See http://www.uri.edu/facsen/428CAC.html for the 438th Report of the Curricular Affairs Committee, Faculty Senate Bill #04-05--9).
The Executive Committee drafted a charge to and membership of the committee in consultation with the Provost and appointed the committee for 2005-06.

Recommendation The Executive Committee recommends approval of the following new sections of the UNIVERSITY MANUAL: 5.83.10 The Providence Campus Undergraduate Initiative Committee shall oversee undergraduate programs offered on the Providence Campus to students admitted under the provisions of section 8.88.10.
The committee shall provide advice and support to the Vice Provost for Urban Programs and the Vice Provost for Academic Affairs during the initial stage of the initiative.
After the establishment phase, the committee shall review the initiative every 4 years.
Specific degree programs will be reviewed every three years on a staggered basis in accordance with the University’s current review policies. 5.83.11 The committee shall be comprised of the following members: one faculty member appointed by each department which offers an

undergraduate program at the Providence Campus; three faculty members appointed by the Faculty Senate in consultation with the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs from departments that do not offer undergraduate programs; and a designee of each of the following: the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs, the Vice Provost for Urban Programs, the Dean of University College and Special Academic Programs and the Dean of Admissions.
Faculty members shall be appointed for three-year staggered terms.
One of the Faculty Senate’s appointees shall serve as chair. 5.83.12 The committee shall meet on a regular basis and report annually to the Faculty Senate through the Curricular Affairs Committee on the status of the overall Providence Campus initiative.
Recommendations shall be forwarded to the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs and the Faculty Senate Curricular Affairs Committee for appropriate action.
II.AMENDING THE UNIVERSITY CALENDAR Background On May 9, 2005, the Faculty Senate approved a revised calendar for academic years through 2010.

Early in the summer it came to the Faculty Senate Executive Committee’s attention that the change in the official date of spring break for 2006 in the approved calendar for 2005-06 created serious confusion and uncertainty for members of the university community.
The change was from the traditional week (March 13-19, 2006), which had been published and promulgated previously, to the following week - March 20-26, 2006.
As people learned of this change in spring break scheduling, a number of problems were identified.
These problems especially affect those members of the campus who must make plans, schedules, travel arrangements, etc., at least one year in advance.
In order to avoid further confusion, the Executive Committee took the unprecedented step of acting for the Senate in accordance with section 4.3 of the Faculty Senate By-Laws and changing the spring semester calendar.
It was agreed that while such action was necessary at that time, the problems that occurred with regard to a last-minute calendar change should not happen again.
As a result, the Executive Committee proposes that, except for emergencies, it should not be possible to modify an approved calendar within 18 months of the start of the semester in question.

Recommendation The Executive Committee recommends approval of a clarification to section 8.70.13 (change is underlined) and the addition of a new section 8.70.14 as follows: 8.70.13 Recommendations regarding rescheduling class days missed within an academic year as the result of natural calamity, work stoppage, etc. shall be the responsibility of the Academic Standards and Calendar Committee, whose proposals will be subject to the approval of the Faculty Senate. 8.70.14 With the exception of circumstances stated in 8.70.13, changes to the calendar shall not be considered within eighteen months prior to the beginning of a semester.

PROPOSAL: THE HONORS INSTITUTE Organizational Change – Creation of Honors Institute and Addition to Chapter 3 The Honors Program proposes expanding its scope and consolidating its operations under a new aegis, the Honors Institute.
The new institute contains the Honors Program, the Honors Colloquium, and the Office of National Fellowships and Academic Opportunities – entities that already fall ad hoc under the umbrella of “Honors.” The creation of the Honors Institute will require organizational change.
It will reside in Chapter 3 of the University Manual.
The Executive Director of the Honors Institute shall be responsible for its oversight and report to the Provost.
The Executive Director and Assistant Executive Director of the Honors Institute shall be the Director and Assistant Director of the Honors Program.
An Advisory Council will be appointed by the Executive Director of the Honors Institute to include faculty representatives from Colleges across the University, Honors student leadership, and major external stakeholders.

The Honors Institute will not figure in Chapter 8 under “Centers and Institutes” (8.90.10-8.90.40) since the Honors Institute, an academic institute, is not the type of institute that this section was intended to govern.
The Honors Program is only one entity housed under the umbrella structure of the Honors Institute.
University Manual language [8.60.10-8.65.12] remains unchanged, including: ● Program Direction and Development.
The Director of the Honors Program in collaboration with the Teaching, Advising, and Assessment Committee shall be responsible for overseeing the Honors Program (8.64.10) ● “The Teaching, Advisement and Assessment Committee shall conduct periodic evaluations of the Honors Program and its separate components” [8.64.12].
Rationale for the creation of an Honors Institute In its current form, “Honors” at URI is minimally competitive with Honors education at our peer flagship institutions.

First, Honors education at URI largely does not meet national best practices and standards in terms of curriculum. (The Honors Program directors will be submitting a redesigned curriculum to the Faculty Senate soon.) Second, and more important to this proposal: The “Honors” ecosystem – the Honors Program, the Honors Colloquium, and the Office of National Fellowships and Academic Opportunities – is minimally integrated into the larger University, which has resulted in a lack of visibility and support.
In their “External Review Report” in 2023, National Collegiate Honors Council reviewers recognized that a transformation into an honors college was not feasible due to financial constraints at URI.
To compete with honors colleges all around us, and to house a 21st-century Honors Program, they recommended establishing an Honors Institute that pulls together officially the Honors Program, the Honors Colloquium, and the Office of National Fellowships and Academic Opportunities.
This highly visible and fully integrated entity would operate on par with the colleges and thus enhance operational efficiency.

The reviewers stated that the creation of a formal Honors Institute will “result in significant long-term returns to the University by raising its academic profile, by attracting a portion of the large number of high-achieving students who are available in the wider area but do not choose to attend URI, and by increasing the amount of annual giving to URI.” Further still, the external reviewers affirm that the success of an Honors Institute “could have ripple effects that launch the University of Rhode Island toward the highest tier of institutions in the Northeast.” Budget The Honors Institute will keep its existing budget infrastructure.
This includes a Fund 100 base budget and external Foundation funding.
The current internal funding is sufficient for the Institute’s operations.
In the shift to an IBB model, Honors will be classified as a central service; we anticipate no decrease in levels of funding to Honors operations.

University Manual language for Chapter 3 3.60.10 The Honors Institute contains the Honors Program (see 8.60.10 - 8.65.12) and the Office of National Fellowships and Academic Opportunities. 3.60.11 The Executive Director of the Honors Institute shall report to the Provost and Executive Vice President for Academic Affairs, and shall have primary responsibility for administering the policies and procedures of this administrative unit. 3.60.12 The Executive Director shall be a non-voting ex officio member of the Honors Program Curriculum and Advisory Committee. Honors contracts are formal agreements facilitated by an honors program, between a student and instructor.

Considering the Honors Contract as an Effective Tool for Furthering Honors Education at URI SUMMARY This document briefly explores the concept of honors contracts, formal agreements facilitated by an honors program, uniting students and instructors to enhance non-honors courses to an hon- ors level through additional work tailored to the “broader, deeper and more complex” learning experiences advocated by the National Collegiate Honors Council (NCHC).
Contracts are recog- nized by over 60% of honors programs in the USA, where they foster community and ownership, enhancing the educational process and commitment to the programs’ success.
Successful honors contracts depend on effective setup, management, and assessment at the hon- ors administration level.
Customization to students’ and faculty interests is essential, providing personalized educational journeys and one-on-one time with instructors.
Students looking to set up contracts should follow a structured approach, guided by honors administration.

This could include early communication about opportunities, advising to educate students on the process and benefits, and encouraging them to approach advisors when identify- ing contract possibilities.
Initiating the process involves engaging with faculty, guided by advis- ing, before registration.
Detailed contracts specifying the project, its outcomes, deadlines, and contact schedules, ensure clarity.
Faculty handle grading, with the honors organization approving credits.
Contracts should bridge the gap between honors and non-honors classrooms, maintaining high standards and clear expectations.
To ensure the effectiveness of honors contracts, too routine or casual use must be prevented.
They should complement, not replace, the program’s curriculum, while preserving community and support.
Faculty involvement should be incentivized and re- warded to maintain a dynamic and successful contract system.

Honors contracts provide flexibility for students to align their education with their interests and goals and allow programs to meet student needs when constraints of students or faculty numbers or funding limitations do not allow honors courses to be run that answer to their interests and needs.
This empowers students, fosters motivation, and facilitates mentor-mentee relationships with faculty. ~KA NOTES ON HONORS CONTRACTS KARL ASPELUND, ASSOCIATE DIRECTOR, URI HONORS OCTOBER 23, 2023

WHAT IS AN HONORS CONTRACT?
AN HONORS CONTRACT is a signed agreement between a student and in- structor.
Facilitated by the honors program, the contract states that the student will complete a specified project in addition to other coursework required and thus “convert” the non-honors class to an honors-equivalent course through additional work, such as outside reading, independent research, or some other enhanced learning activity (Badenhausen, 7).
Usually, students are required to earn both an A or B grade for the regular coursework and submit acceptable contract work to qualify for honors credit. (James, 30) A little over 60% of honors programs in the USA—regardless of institutional type—use contracts (Bahls, 172.) CONTRACTS provide an extra measure of curricular flexibility at institutions that are not able to field enough faculty, cannot provide an adequate number of honors courses, or do not have a large enough of a student body to fill hon- ors sections.
Contracts can fill the gap and provide opportunities for students’ self-guided intellectual growth (Bahls, 175).

For example, work at the University Honors Program at the University of Kan- sas shows that honors contracts act as far more than stopgaps to address honors course shortages.
They can “facilitate access to honors, increase completion, democratize key aspects of the honors experience, provide students with struc- tured avenues for building relationships with faculty members, and empower students to own their educational experiences” (Dotter, 56).
Honors contracts not only maximize faculty-student contact in classes of any format, they also accommodate exploration and questioning in a range of research disciplines, from team-taught humanities discussions to innovative in- vestigations in STEM courses, including their labs (Myers and Whitebread, 22.) Further, as a valued part of honors education, tutorial-based contracts can be seen as a special approach used in various modes of learning: Research and creative scholarship, breadth and enduring questions, service learning and leadership, experiential learning, and learning communities.

They can therefore similarly result in the “broader, deeper, and more complex learning-centered and learner-directed experiences” with which the NCHC defines honors educa- tion (Myers and Whitebread, 40 & NCHC Shared Principles and Practices).
WHY USE HONORS CONTRACTS?
Provide an extra measure of curricular flexibility Empower students to their own learning experiences Maximize faculty-student contact Result in broader, deeper, and more complex learning centered and learner direct- ed experiences An agreement, mediated by the honors program, be- tween student and instructor that defines further work that“converts” the non-hon- ors class to an honors equivalent course. 60+ % of programs use contracts 2 Honors education is characterized by in-class and extracurricular activities that are measurably broader, deeper, or more complex than comparable learn - ing experiences typically found at institutions of higher education.

Honors expe - riences include a distinctive learner-directed environment and philosophy, pro - vide opportunities that are appropriately tailored to fit the institution’ s culture and mission, and frequently occur within a close community of students and faculty. ~National Collegiate Honors Council: Definition of Honors Education

HOW ARE CONTRACTS SET UP EFFECTIVELY?
A COMPREHENSIVE SET OF GUIDELINES, that include the basic expecta- tions of the honors experience and specific expectations for contracting, should be available and presented to students early on.
These should include that two of the primary purposes of contracting are to: 1) enable a student and faculty member to establish a one-to-one, ongoing mentor-mentee relationship through- out the semester and 2) to enable the student to experience the subject matter in more depth. (Bolsch, 54) Three honors-related dissertations reporting mixed experiences with contracts find or imply that students appreciate contracts when they meet two conditions: 1) student and faculty customize the work to fit a student’s interests, and 2) con- tracts involve significant time with the instructor (Myers and Whitebread: 23) Faculty members should be solely responsible for assigning course grades.
However, the contracting process should be structured from the outset as one in which the honors organization certifies that a successfully contracted course should be designated for “honors credit” on a student’s transcript.

So, while the faculty member assigns the grade for the course based on requirements unrelat- ed to the contract, honors administration is responsible for placing, essentially, a “seal of approval” on each contract experience through an additional transcript notation once it receives the faculty member’s certification that the elements of the contract were completed. (See: Bolsch, 52) Creating databases for honors advisors of all past digital contracts, searchable by course and faculty mentor’s name can lead to more proactive advising about innovative approaches to contracts and increased access to examples before students even meet with faculty. (Thomas & Hunter, 242) THE A V AILABILITY AND BENEFITS OF CONTRACTS need to be careful- ly publicized to newly-arrived honors students.
Honors advisors should initially help students understand where in their trajec- tory an honors contract might be instrumental and beneficial.
It should be made clear how important a dialogue with instructors will be, and how much this relies on student initiative and their own vision for their learning.

Honors administration and advisors should promote that students, immediate- ly on identifying a course within which they´d be interested to do contracted work, that they talk with an honors advisor to ensure that they understand the process and are aware of their options. “These meetings allow students to re- hearse future conversations with faculty in a safe environment, enable advisors to set clear expectations for contracts, and equip students with the necessary language to meet those expectations” (Dotter, 59.) Students should approach instructors before registering to discuss options and get a firm commitment so the contract is viable and that the honors credits they are receiving that term will be sufficient for their continuing success.
HOW SHOULD STUDENTS APPROACH SETTING UP A CONTRACT?
Searchable databases of past digital contracts lead to more proactive advising Publicize contracts early and often!
Encourage students to ap- proach advisors as soon as they see an opportunity for a contract arise.

Students must approach faculty—with the help of ad- vising— before registering to begin the process Two primary purposes: Enabling a mentor-mentee relationship and a more in-depth experience of the subject matter Students appreciate con- tracts that are fitted to their interests and afford signifi- cant time with the instructor Faculty assign grades, the honors organization ap- proves the honors credits and notifies Enrollment Services.
Advise students early on about the process and bene- fits of contracts 3
WHAT MIGHT A CONTRACT STIPULATE?

FIVE COMPONENTS should be, at least, required for a contract: 1) A substantial (15-20 p.) paper or project (of equivalent time/effort: c. 20 hours) should be defined and outlined. 2) It should be required that the student share the knowledge/skills/experienc- es gained through the paper or project with an audience, either in the class or elsewhere. 3) The contract should include a plan for how the faculty member and student have regular contact outside of class to discuss the student’s progress and an- swer questions regarding the paper or project. 4)The student should be required to state specifically on the contract form how they will meet each of the three NCHC requirements of “broader, deeper, more complex.” 5) A date at the midpoint of the semester should be determined at which the faculty member should provide a brief report to honors administration on the contact they have had with the student and assess the student’s progress to date. (See: Bolsch 2005: 55) CONTRACTS EXEMPLIFY THE BEST OF HONORS PEDAGOGY when, anchored in the tutorial model, they cultivate personalized, mentored learning and ensure consistent, documented quality (Myers and Whitebread, 22).

It is therefore important that honors administrators and advisors keep a close eye on the contracts created, their implementation, and progress, and provide solid templates and rubrics for their creation and use.
While contract courses do not always provide a venue for honors students to interact with each other, they do create space for students to collaborate with instructors and develop important mentoring relationships (Wyatt, 215).
This outcome–a “win-win” if well managed–must be continually emphasized to both faculty and students.
An inclusive pedagogical practice opens the curriculum to a wide array of fac- ulty who become stakeholders in honors.
It has been shown that these curricular practices have led to greater acceptance of and appreciation for honors colleges on campuses where faculty participation is widespread (Wyatt, 196).
Honors administration must therefore constantly work toward an awareness of these practices among all faculty at the University, whether they teach honors students or not.
WHAT ARE EXAMPLES OF POSITIVE OUT- COMES FROM THE USE OF CONTRACTS?

Contracts must be well managed and assessed at the honors admin. level so that they be the effective tool that they are.
Contracts foster and sup- port a sense of community and ownership around hon- ors programs.
The contract should define the contracted project, its deliverables and intended outcomes and deadlines, as well as points of contact and required feedback by the faculty supervisor.
Maintain the awareness that contracts are a venue for meaningful student-faculty relationships. 4

WHAT ARE EXAMPLES OF POSSIBLE PROBLEMS THAT APPEAR WHEN USING CONTRACTS AND WHAT ARE PATHS TOW ARD AVOIDING THEM?
PROBLEMS THAT APPEAR ARE NOT INSURMOUNTABLE.
Mostly they are cir- cumvented by a continuing awareness of processes and a care for good structures and assessment, creating contracts that enhance rather than concede the honors experience (Bambina, 122).
Contracts must not become “routine” or commonplace, no matter what their number.
Nor can they become a “secret fix” only available to those “in the know.” The narrow definition of honors programs can lead to charges of elitism and segre- gation if honors students, who increasingly tend to be upper-middle-class, white, and female, become insulated from the general student population in an honors curricular bubble.
The contract approach mitigates this by allowing students to learn in an in- clusive campus-wide environment while still engaging in an honors curriculum and community (Wyatt, 196).
Overworked instructors may agree to contracts but then require little more than comple- tion of extra assignments with minimal instructor-student interaction.

Honors educators have the responsibility to eliminate underdeveloped honors contracts that dilute rather than enrich the academic experiences of students. (Wyatt, 195.) It is good practice for evaluation and assessment templates to be created and provided by the honors organiza- tion.
And oversight of contracts by honors administrators must therefore be well-struc- tured, mandated, and clear, and guidelines must be provided to faculty on deadlines and assessment rubrics.
It is essential that contracted work not simply be “more”; rather, it must be meaningful- ly integrated in each case with the course content and learning goals and the work the course already requires. (Bahls, 177) The contract must therefore measurably outline work that leads to the “broader, deeper, and more complex learning-centered and learn- er-directed experiences” with which the NCHC defines honors education (NCHC).

The suggestion that the learning experience of a contracted class is equivalent to a stand-alone honors class—seeing as the student receives academic credit for both— opens honors programs and colleges up to potential exploitation by administrators who may not see the need for assigning appropriate resources to honors or may even try to cut budgets. (Badenhausen, 11) It must therefore be agreed—and practiced—that when options are limited, contracts are a workable path to honors completion that benefits both the students and the institution, not a work-around for the program or institution to avoid curriculum development and creating classes.
But even though the close community of students and faculty that defines honors edu- cation is achieved here by other means, the importance of achieving a sense of belong- ing to the larger cohort should not be ignored.
Therefore, a stricture should be in place that students be limited in the number of credits they can complete through contracts, especially in their freshman and sophomore years.

Finally, with increasing demands and tightening budgets overburdening faculty with unpaid work that is not recognized in reviews, it is essential that faculty be recognized and compensated for the additional work a contract entails.
Otherwise, faculty fatigue may set in and departments and colleges may resent the outside burdens (Bambina, 118).
The equivalent of a one-credit independent study would seem reasonable, and perhaps an amendment to faculty contracts might state the value of this work for pro- motion and tenure reviews.
Contracts bring honors students into non-honors classrooms, mitigating the separation of honors stu- dents from others.
Contracts are a beneficial part of the honors methods in individual cases, not a substitute for the program.
Students should be a part of an honors cohort, con- tacts should not be allowed to separate them from the group.
Administration must take care to never let contracts become routine or a “secret fix.” Honors admin. must work diligently to maintain high standards, and clear expec- tations Contract-work must mea- surably achieve NCHC goals: broader, deeper, and more complex learning experiences.
Faculty must be rewarded for the work they do, lest fatigue or resentment under- mine the contract system. 5

FACULTY SENATE OFFICE 224 PASTORE HALL, 51 LOWER COLLEGE ROAD, KINGSTON, RI 02881 USA, P: 401.874.2616 NOVEMBER 7, 2024 Dear Senators, Our community at-large and the faculty senate are both committed to protecting expressive speech as a core right underpinning academic freedom at the University of Rhode Island.
The recent DRAFT University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees Regulations Regarding Use of University Property, if approved without revision, would undermine this right.
It girds an overly vague set of conditions for the use of property with punitive consequences to be administered with vague guidelines and unfettered power.
Despite the inclusion of language which emphasizes learning, the letter makes no specific reference to academic freedom or its prominence in our University Manual (Chapter 6).
In this letter, I summarize the phases of the regulation's evolution over the past several months, as far as I am aware.
Then, I provide a short summary of the major concerns about the regulation that senators and other community members have identified.
Finally, I outline next steps.

Timeline • Spring/Summer 2024: Various communications from the URI administration indicated that lack of a policy pertaining to protest and its potential harms, particularly with respect to university property, was a concern. • Late August 2024: In writing, I requested senate review of policy drafts given potential bearing on academic life.
I received no reply in advance of the below steps. • Early October 2024: The DRAFT regulations were presented to the Administrative Policy Committee (on which I sit as Senate President) by Vice President of Administration and Finance (VPAF) Benson.
The DRAFT regulation was supplied one hour.
I raised concerns about austerity and potential impacts at the meeting, despite having to comment in real-time.
It was posted for public comment by the next day. • Mid-October 2024: Concerns arise in the community following communications to union members by the AAUP-URI executive director. • Late October 2024: Senate leadership meets with the VPAF and her staff.
The parties tentatively agree to participate in an ad hoc committee to assist with redress of the substantive problems, in addition to holding a forum at the next senate meeting.

Process issues about how these policies were shared and not properly vetted will be addressed at a future time.
Major Concerns Many senators have written to me by email or posted comments (400+) to the VPAFs policy site.
Of these, I am attaching four letters from senators and faculty, as well as a comment

written by the Rhode Island ACLU Executive Director and sent to the VPAF on the matter.
At a minimum, the following major areas of concern have been cited as areas of major concern around the proposed regulation. • The need for a policy or regulation to react to protest events on a campus that has essentially never seen violent protest, and which has a tradition of peaceful, participatory, and deliberative discourse, is ostensibly undocumented. • The policy is very vague on how response to property damage events will be pursued.
References to other handbooks, manuals, contracts, and laws seem to have been sufficient to manage any event involving damage to property in the past.

It is not clear how these policies will be enacted differently under this regulation, or if they should be. • Even if the regulation is stood up, there is a seemingly draconian presentation of severe punishments bereft of clear attendant policy, due process, and collective participation of appropriate university bodies. • There is a clear lack of common sense considerations in the regulation, such as faculty not being able to access their labs in off-hours, punishments for simple infractions such as littering with a flyer, and so on. • The forceful, top-down style, in the document and in procedural choices, contrasts starkly with the norms of a community that prides itself on academic freedom, constructive expressive speech, and civility, and with the expectations of a senate that is an equal partner in shared governance.
Charge to Attend and Engage Modern universities should form an intellectually safe, free marketplace of ideas.
Our faculty and students need to be able to express themselves without the weight of oppressive and potentially life altering consequences hanging over their heads while engaging in study, life and work.

This is especially true for our students who are learning to use their voices for change and good.
This DRAFT regulation is clearly not in-line with these imperatives.
Our task is to ensure that these issues are addressed through our deliberations and advocacy, and, if necessary, through legislation.
Please join us at the next Faculty Senate meeting on November 14 at 3:00 PM in the Hope Room, Higgins Welcome Center, at which time this matter will be discussed.
There are other important topics on the agenda, and many people will wish to speak on this matter, so please come prepared with concise statements.
We will not be addressing matters of university and senate process around policies and regulations at this meeting; however, we will be considering this need at another time.
Sincerely, Theodore (Ted) Walls URI Faculty Senate President, 2024-2025

Senator Koray Ozpolat 10/15/2024 Comments on the proposed regulations regarding the use of university property In principle, I agree that the university may establish reasonable standards and limitations regarding time, place and manner of use for university property.
Most of the listed limitations and prohibited activities (2a-2o) look reasonable.
However, I have three concerns (i) 2g. signs, posting and banners (ii) 3.
Enforcements and Violations, (iii) the timing of this proposal Motivation “Academic institutions exist for the transmission of knowledge, the pursuit of truth, the development of students, and the general well-being of society.
Free inquiry and free expression are indispensable to the attainment of these goals. “(AAUP Joint Statement) I believe it is important that URI remains an open space for students, faculty, and staff to exchange ideas and express themselves.
While protecting the university property matters, our strategic goal is to develop young minds to think critically and globally.

That’s how we can develop the leaders of the future who will “commit to addressing the most pressing issues facing our state and the global community” as mentioned in URI’s Strategic Priority-1 Concerns I am worried that with “somewhat” restrictive property policies and harsh sanctions for violations, the proposed regulations may broadly discourage students and faculty from engaging in campus activism, protests and demonstrations.
For example, if a student affixes a poster or a sign to the exterior of a building, could s/he face disciplinary action up to termination?
I would say “let them post” and URI employees can pull unauthorized posters later.
Why punish our students?
I am concerned about the timing of this proposal too.
What events put this proposal forward?
To the best of my knowledge, we did not have any encampments, or damage to campus property this year.
Is our administration under pressure from donors or politicians?
Conclusion After 13 years at URI, it is clear to me that political violence or destruction of campus property are not big issues in Kingston but on the contrary, it is lack of dissent and weak activism that slows down the growth of our students.

Many URI students have no idea or don’t care about what is going on beyond their small worlds!
Any policy that directly/indirectly discourages (the already weak) campus activism and demonstrations actually hurts the development of our students and I propose that • 2g is removed • The disciplinary actions for other violations be clarified • URI Administration shares with us - why now, justify the need for these restrictions • The introduction paragraph of the document can be extended to underline freedom of speech & assembly as vital elements of academic freedom and that buildings partially serve this purpose.

Thoughts on draft regulations for use of URI property: The draft is very legalistic and very top-down; it is “command-and-control” in tone.
The subtext of the regulations is that misbehavior will not be tolerated.
I’m not sure that is an eCective message to control the members of a University community.
The Introduction does not mention the special role of the University as a place where dissent is protected, and where the interruption of normal activities by peaceful civil disobedience is accepted for its potential contribution to civic discourse and social change.
As a place that honors free speech, the University should project collegiality and respect, even in laying down rules.
Some prohibitions in the draft are unnecessarily granular, treating such things as discarded leaﬂets (litter), impeding traCic, hanging banners, etc., which might occur during demonstrations, as punishable oCences.
History shows that prohibition of minor and incidental acts is often an invitation to law-breaking and/or an excuse to arrest, rather than an eCective way of controlling behavior.

It should also be noted that such prohibitions foster cynicism and undermine the trust of community members in their leaders and their pride in representing the institution.
The option of achieving community peace through consultation and dialogue with parties in conﬂict is not mentioned.
However, this is a far more eCective way to achieve the apparent goals of the draft, without threats and without talking down to the University community.
I recommend that: (1) this draft be revised in a negotiation process involving several sectors of the University community (administrators, staC, faculty, student organizations).
The revision should seek a balance between the administration’s control needs and recognition of the University’s special role in society as a place where dissent is protected; (2) minor, symbolic, and incidental acts be removed from the list of chargeable oCences; and (3) exceptions to the rules laid down be granted either in writing or verbally.

Thomas Zorabedian, Ed.D.
Adjunct Professor, Film/Media and Honors Program Former Assistant Dean, URI College of Arts & Sciences zman@uri.edu RE: Proposed “Regulations Regarding Use of University Property” At its best, a university is a marketplace of ideas.
These ideas may be, and often are, diverse and contradictory, or even at times contentious.
At its weakest, universities discourage or even squelch the free exchange of opinions, beliefs, and feelings.
I recall a time, including specifically at URI, when students and faculty regularly embraced the former approach and engaged in lively interactions.
I fear that the trend in general seems to be in a different direction of less tolerance for public and disparate engagement on campus.
To this end, parts of the proposed regulations raise some concerns that they are not entirely in keeping with the university’s mission which specifically refers to “the freedom to learn” and the “dissemination of new knowledge aimed at contributing to the public good.” Most of the regulations regarding the “control and use” of the university property seem reasonable, sensible, and even innocuous.

Of course, I agree that the destruction, defacing, and vandalizing of property and violation of various laws should be prohibited.
However, two sections include language that could unnecessarily restrict the freedom of expression, and in fact could discourage or even severely punish those who choose to express and share their ideas: 2(f): “Leafletting and Distribution of Literature.” The proposal only allows this time-tested approach “provided that the activity does not impede the flow of pedestrian or vehicular traffic…or create litter.” What exactly does this mean?
Is this a major problem?
While no one should force material on anyone, does going up to someone while they are walking and stopping to give them material “impede” them?
And, if someone who is given some material throws it away, is the person handing it out in violation of littering?
These are not irrelevant questions, because section 3 refers to “suspension or expulsion” as a possible enforcement, a draconian response. 2(g): “Signs, Posters, Banners.” Again, signs that create permanent or temporary damage should not be allowed.

But, could students who attach a sign or drape a banner to a wall, dorm balcony, or building be suspended or expelled, as per section 3?
URI has had innumerable instances over the years of students displaying sentiments or slogans, with the intent of “contributing to the public good,” with no damage to university property.
In fact, the lack of such signage has been conspicuous over the last decade or so.
Further, this section states that “no signs supported by standards or sticks shall be permitted in any assembly inside any building.” If this were a regulation at our country’s national conventions, a good percentage of the attendees would have been thrown out or arrested.
I assume the concern is that a “stick” may become a weapon of some kind.
Obviously, that kind of usage should not be tolerated and should be dealt with harshly.
However, because signs and banners are often held up by some means of support, it follows that the peaceful use of this method of expression should be allowed.
Further, it would be refreshing to see more of this on a campus when students usually seem uninvolved in political, cultural, or social issues.

While I understand that damage to university property can be costly, time-consuming, and aesthetically disagreeable, one of the great and important traditions and freedoms of university life, including at URI, since the late 1960s has been the thoughtful sharing and display of ideas and information.
We should do what we can to encourage that essential aspect of learning, rather than develop new ways to suppress it.
Respectfully submitted, Thomas Zorabedian

4 November 2024 Dr.
Theodore Walls, Faculty Senate President URI Faculty Senate Executive Committee Dear Ted: Per the request of FSEC to provide comments on a proposed University Regulation under consideration by the Senate and the wider URI community, I offer the following observations.
In Section 2 of the proposed regulation there is a listing of Limitations and Prohibited Activities.
In many of these prohibited practices, there is a tacit disregard for the tools by which those with less power within established social hierarchies can express their point of view with enough impact to effectively communicate with powerful decision makers.
As Frederick Douglas once wrote, “Power concedes nothing without a demand.
It never did and it never will.” The University of Rhode Island largely since the Presidency of Francis Horn in the 1960s has strongly embraced a principles of community free speech in opposition of national public policies such as the Vietnam War, and in the late 1970s in response to unfair state labor practices.
Notably, the former provost Beverly Swan (of Swan Hall fame) was a prominent protester staffing the luncheon buffets set up during the high-profile faculty strike.

Moreover, there has been effective protest of university policies that have led to meaningful positive changes at URI.
In the early 1990s, effective protests by the “Brothers United” occupied Taft Hall over civil rights issues and greater emphasis on racial equity at URI.
There was effective communication to President Carothers and the RI Board of Governors for Higher Education that something was very wrong at URI in race relations.
President Carothers then went on to establish the Multicultural Center in the center of campus.
It seems reasonable to prohibit violence or endangerment to others by university regulation, but some other proposed regulations may constitute only a minor nuisance to community members.
These proposed regulations include disruption of meetings, impeding building entry for a while, etc. might be tolerated for a time and resolved by official dialog.
Various other practices listed for possible prohibition could be construed as ordinary vigorous expressions of free speech, including leafleting, signs, posters, banners, erection of structures, camping overnight as part of protest action although a nuisance.
Nuisance is the point!

Why would protesters go through the bother unless they felt something important to say?
Picking up after protesters is not much different than cleaning up after a football game.
The one of the most egregious “Catch 22s” of the proposed regulation is in item o, “Sanitation.
Outdoors” in which defecation or urination is prohibited.
This seems reasonable at first glance, but this item is accompanied by item k, Building Access, where all the restrooms are located.
One might avail of a sanitation company to bring in temporary latrines to service protesters, but this

might be construed as violating item i “Erection of Structures”, requiring permission of the VP. What if the VP is not sympathetic to the cause of the protesters and denies permission to protest? Could the bodily functions be used as a weapon against sustained free speech activities? One of the most prominent non-sequiturs in the proposed regulations is item m, prohibiting bicycles, skateboards and other conveyances on campus. In an era of developing alternatives to fossil fuels, any sort of carbon-free transport to the university from outside and within the university should be encouraged rather than discouraged. Perhaps a joint senate and administration effort to develop vehicular traffic norms around campus may be a more effective strategy of maintaining pedestrian safety. Thank you for this opportunity to comment. Sincerely, Michael A. Rice, PhD Faculty Senator, CELS

COMMENTS ON PROPOSED UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND BOARD OF TRUSTEES REGULATIONS REGARDING USE OF UNIVERSITY PROPERTY October 2024 The American Civil Liberties Union of Rhode Island appreciates the opportunity to offer comments on the Board of Trustees’ proposed regulations regarding University Property . We understand that they are designed to convey the University of Rhode Island’s commitment to quality education through the use and protection of its University Property. Some provisions in these proposed regulations, however, also have a deleterious effect, even if unintentional, on the University’s concomitant commitment to protecting academic freedom and the First Amendment rights of students. It is with the goal of safeguarding those rights that we offer the following comments for consideration. The Proposed Regulations 1. Section 2(a). Individual Rights: This section prevents using University Property “in a manner that impinges upon the rights of another person under the United States or Rhode Island Constitution; any federal, state, or local law; or any University policy.” While one cannot argue with this goal in the abstract, we are concerned about its potential misuse in implementation. On university campuses across the country, we have recently seen conflicts where student speech on political matters is said – often unfairly, in our view – to impinge on the rights of other students to feel safe or free from discrimination. We believe 128 Dorrance Street, Suite 400 Providence, RI 02903 Phone: (401) 831-7171 Fax: (401) 831-7175 www.riaclu.org info@riaclu.org

2 this provision must better define when use of University Property “impinges upon the rights of another person” in order to avoid confusion and disputes about its potential application to unpopular, but constitutionally protected, opinions or speech by either faculty or students. 2.
Section 2(e).
Endangerment: This section prohibits the use of University Property to “endanger” others.
The word “endanger” is undefined, which leaves it open to wide interpretation and, again, potentially applicable to protected speech.
We would urge that the wording be clarified to explicitly refer to physical endangerment. 3.
Section 2(f).
Leafletting and Distribution of Literature: This section would allow the university to bar leafletting or distribution of literature if it “create[s] litter.” This is extremely problematic and should be stricken.
The exercise of free speech rights cannot be prohibited because of the improper behavior of others.
Littering by students who receive a leaflet is out of the control of the distributor, yet this provision would allow for the denial of the leafleteer’s First Amendment rights on the basis of a third party’s actions.
For close to a century, the U.S.

Supreme Court has rejected such efforts.1 Also, while leafletters should not be allowed to block access to buildings or walkways while engaged in this quintessential First Amendment activity, we are concerned that the rule’s ban on “impeding” the flow of pedestrian traffic could be interpreted in an overly restrictive manner.
After all, any distribution of literature has the potential to contribute to temporary bottlenecks, but that should not serve as a basis for prohibiting it. 1 As far back as 1939, the Court noted: “We are of opinion that the purpose to keep the streets clean and of good appearance is insu=icient to justify an ordinance which prohibits a person rightfully on a public street from handing literature to one willing to receive it. . . .
There are obvious methods of preventing littering.
Amongst these is the punishment of those who actually throw papers on the streets.” Schneider v.
State, 308 U.S. 147, 162 (1939).

3 We urge that this wording be modified so as to bar, for exam ple, leafletting only if it “significantly” impedes the flow of traffic.
This section also gives Housing and Residential Life and Dining Services the ability to develop additional leafletting restrictions for areas under their control.
This provision should require those departments to explicitly articulate their rationale for any additional restrictions and ensure that they are narrowly crafted to address the specific issue warranting these extra limitations.
Indeed, from our perspective, one might expect residential facilities at the school to have fewer, not greater, restrictions. 4.
Section 2(g).
Signs, Postings, Banners: This section limits the posting of signs to designated areas of University Property, specifically “designated bulletin boards or other areas identified for positing [sic].” In line with our comments on Section 2(f), we would urge that this be clarified to exempt dormitory rooms and related areas within those buildings.

For example, a student who wishes to display a banner from a window either inside or outside their dorm room, or to post a political sign on their door, should be allowed to do so without fear of punishment.
The University should not have the discretion to determine whether such areas are “designated” for posting signs.
In addition, if the locations that the University “designates” for sign posting are insufficiently prevalent or unduly restrictive, this rule could severely impac t communication between students for purposes of noticing meetings, rallies or other events.
We recommend that the rules provide a process to allow students to formally petition to have a location be deemed a designated area for posting information beyond those set out initially by the University.

4 5.
Section 2(i).
Erection of Structures: This section prohibits erecting both permanent and temporary structures without specific written permission.
The scope of “temporary structures” should be defined and limited.
If a “structure” is erected for a minimum period of time in concert with a political protest or similar activity, written permission should not be required any more than the temporary use of open university space itself for a spontaneous protest or rally.
These situations are very different from the type of encampment concerns that this rule seems to be aimed at , but they would be treated identically as this rule is presently worded. 6.
Section 2(k).
Building Access: This section grants the University the right to ask guests in residential buildings “to leave at any time.” This completely standardless authority to order guests to leave is quite inappropriate.
The policy should have a “good cause” requirement and specify the types of conduct that would authorize the University to remove a guest from a residential building.
A broad “in loco parentis” standard is simply anachronistic and unwarranted in the university setting. 7.
Section 3.

Enforcement and Violations: This section states that violations of any of these policies can result in various disciplinary actions, including the imposition of fines.
The section specifies that the Board of Trustees derives authority to impose fines from RIGL §16-32-2.
However, that statute allows a “district or police court,” not the University, to impose fines for violations of school policies.
Furthermore, under this section, the user of the University Property is deemed responsible for any property damage that is incurred, even if the user did not cause the damage.
For example, if a protest takes place on campus and a counter-protester throws a

5 rock through a window, the organizer – and not the protester who threw the rock – would be held responsible under this section. It should be revised to avoid any such scenario. In sum, the ACLU believes it is important that these rules be revised to be more mindful of their potential impact and infringement on the exercise of First Amendment rights, and that they make clear that they can be applied to speech activity only in accordance with the time, place and manner restrictions appropriate for a public or limited public forum. Thank you for your consideration of our views. We trust that they will be given your careful consideration. Submitted by: Steven Brown, Executive Director American Civil Liberties Union of Rhode Island
